drills.q: Why is DCO better framed as a bandit problem than a static A/B test?
drills.a: Creative performance is non-stationary -- it fatigues over time. A bandit continuously reallocates traffic and can pull back from a decaying 'winner' in near-real time, unlike a fixed-horizon test that makes one discrete decision at the end.

drills.q: What heuristic signals commonly flag creative fatigue?
drills.a: CTR decline of roughly 10%+, CPA rise of roughly 15%+, and impression frequency exceeding roughly 3 per user in prospecting campaigns -- category-dependent heuristics, not universal constants.

drills.q: Why does full-combination DCO across many creative components hit a traffic wall?
drills.a: Each unique combination needs roughly the per-arm sample size a standalone test would, so total traffic requirement scales with combination count (L^k-style) -- e.g. 4 headlines x 5 images x 3 CTAs = 60 arms needing individual convergence.

drills.q: What do feature-level (component) DCO bandits assume, and when does that assumption break?
drills.a: They assume components combine roughly additively. It breaks when a specific pairing has a real interaction effect the additive model can't capture -- that pairing then needs to be tested as its own dedicated arm.

drills.q: Why doesn't a standard bandit automatically account for creative fatigue?
drills.a: Its reward estimate is an un-decayed average/posterior over all history, implicitly assuming stationary reward. It keeps over-allocating traffic to a fatiguing creative because the historical average lags the true declining trend.

drills.q: Name two mechanisms to make a bandit fatigue-aware, and explain why they're complementary rather than substitutes.
drills.a: Exponential decay/sliding window on the reward estimate (tracks population-level average decline over time) and explicit per-user frequency capping (hard limit guaranteeing no single user gets excessive repeat exposure, independent of the reward signal). Decay alone doesn't protect any specific user from over-exposure, so the two work together.

drills.q: What's the difference between reactive and proactive creative fatigue detection, and why does it matter for spend?
drills.a: Reactive detection fires only after an aggregate metric crosses a threshold, meaning real spend already went to a decaying creative before detection. Proactive detection predicts the decay trajectory from early engagement-curve shape, catching likely fatigue before the lagging metric visibly crosses a threshold, reducing wasted spend.

drills.q: A component-level DCO bandit predicts headline X + image Y should perform well individually but the actual combination underperforms. What's going on and how do you catch this systematically?
drills.a: A real interaction effect the additive component model can't capture -- the same tradeoff fractional-factorial designs accept explicitly. Catch it systematically by periodically spot-checking full combinations against component-model predictions and flagging large residuals as candidates for dedicated per-combination testing.

drills.q: Design a creative optimization system for a campaign with 6 headlines, 8 images, and 4 CTAs (192 combinations) on a moderate traffic budget.
drills.a: Reject full-combination testing given the traffic math. Use a component-level (or low-rank contextual) bandit learning marginal performance per element, composing top-scoring combinations for serving, while periodically spot-checking full combinations against predictions to catch interaction effects. Layer exponential-decay reward estimation and per-user frequency capping for fatigue, and route any auto-generated creative through brand-safety/quality gates before it enters the bandit's action space.

drills.q: What creative-specific bug is a common real-world cause of sample ratio mismatch in creative tests?
drills.a: A broken image asset or truncated headline that fails to render on a specific device/browser for one variant, silently dropping that variant's impressions/clicks in a non-random way across the audience -- the same SRM discipline from experiment design applies directly to creative tests.
